summary:
Bangka-Belitung Islands stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is assessed as a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to one year's imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The provision applies in Bangka-Belitung Islands as throughout Indonesia.

No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and Indonesia has no anti-discrimination or hate-crime provisions for LGBT people. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unrecognised, so no same-sex relationship carries legal recognition anywhere in the country.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, a process that shapes what documents a trans visitor or resident can present at airports, hotels and police checks.

Physical risk is rising across Indonesia. Reporting by The Diplomat in August 2026 describes a transgender community facing growing repression, with vigilante mobs attacking trans people as the government moves to codify anti-LGBT provisions. Reporting in the same period ties the surge in attacks to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. A visitor travelling onward from Bangka-Belitung Islands to either province carries the national exposure plus that provincial layer.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Social and institutional hostility is documented at national level. A 2025 Pew figure found 93% of Indonesians rating homosexuality 'morally unacceptable'. The Constitutional Court rejected a petition to criminalise gay sex on 14 December 2017 by 5-4, and Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025. No deviation from this national position has been documented in Bangka-Belitung Islands.
tangentialFactors:
The national pattern of criminalisation is not uniform across Indonesia's provinces. Aceh and South Sumatra add provincial penalties for same-sex conduct on top of the national penal code, and Aceh's caning sentence of February 2025 shows those provisions are enforced against people present in the province rather than residents alone. Bangka-Belitung Islands has no documented provincial-level deviation in either direction, so the national regime is the operative layer for a visitor there.

Official rhetoric and enforcement are linked in the reporting. The August 2026 account of rising mob violence against transgender Indonesians attributes the escalation to public condemnations by officials and to the October 2025 presidential decree that classifies LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat. The Puncak villa raid of June 2025 shows that private, consensual gatherings remain exposed to police action even where no law is broken.

Custody risk is a distinct factor from street risk. The 2022 death of Rodrigo Ventocilla in Indonesian custody, and the extortion demand reported during his detention, indicate that arrest on any charge carries consequences beyond the charge itself for a foreign national.

Public opinion and the courts point the same way: 93% of Indonesians rated homosexuality morally unacceptable in 2025 polling, and the Constitutional Court's 5-4 refusal to criminalise gay sex in December 2017 was a narrow rejection of expansion, not a protection. Indonesia's votes against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025 place its government in a small international bloc on the question.
localsOnly:
Residents of Bangka-Belitung Islands live under the same national penal code as visitors, including the extra-marital sex provision in force since 2 January 2026, and the same absence of anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Legal gender recognition is available only through sex reassignment surgery followed by a judge's approval, and identity documents carry only 'male' or 'female' markers. There is no third-gender or X descriptor, so a resident's documents cannot reflect a non-binary identity.

Relationship recognition does not exist for same-sex couples: marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are all unavailable, which affects inheritance, hospital access, next-of-kin standing and shared property.

Residents are exposed to the expression provisions as well as conduct provisions. The 2006 pornography law reaches written and audio-visual material suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment, and online content presenting LGBT behaviour was the subject of a bill under discussion in 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports any trans-specific incident, police action, local bylaw or protection measure within Bangka-Belitung Islands itself. The province's entry rests on the national framework and on the absence of any documented deviation from it; territory-level enforcement data is unresolved and not sourced here.

The maximum penalty for the extra-marital sex provision is stated inconsistently across the material available for this record, with one figure of one year's imprisonment and another of two years. The lower figure, matching the cited national source, is used above; the discrepancy is unresolved.

Whether Bangka-Belitung Islands has adopted any provincial or regency-level religious bylaw touching on same-sex conduct or transgender expression is not sourced in this inventory and remains unresolved.

Access to gender-affirming medical care, and any local practice around its provision to residents or visitors in this province, is not covered by the available sources.
